Title: Cost of Card Slot in Player Hand

Messages.Author: rfg...@eos.ncsu.edu
Messages.Body:
That "other" sorta longish thread about errata got me thinking about
what I consider an extra card slot to be worth, say in terms of pool.

Getting started, lets consider Elder Library:

1 Extra Card Slot, 1 Pool, Lasting as long as you are in the game.

The variable here, of course, is how long you will be in the game...
IIRC Robert Goudie did a survey of the LA Tourney scene and found that
games lasted about six turns for each player. I'm going to be a little
more generous and presume that each player gets ten turns. That would
make the card slot from Elder Library worth 1/10 of a pool per turn.

Now, Dreams of the Sphinx:

2 Extra Card Slots, 1 Pool, Not more than three turns total.

The difference here is that You only get the hand size bonus during the
current turn, meaning that I've got to depreciate the pool value of "per
turn" which I just used to mean "from turn to turn". Simple math comes
to 1/6 of a pool, which I'll half to 1/12 of a pool per turn.

The exact number is debatable, but I think anything between 1/6 - 1/12
is a fair number to quote.

From this we can calculate the amount of pool it costs to play
Aggressive Tactics - 2 Pool, 1 Card Slot, (D) Burnable. I've never
played with the card so I don't know how long the card sticks around,
but I'd guess it's high on the "Things to burn" list.

The cost of -just- playing the card would be pool cost minus benefit.

Which if burned after one turn is 2 - (~1/10) or 1 and 9/10 pool.
If burned after three turns is 2/3 - (~1/10) or ~4/7 pool per turn.
At 20 turns the card is free given the benefit you have received, but
the game isn't likely to last that long.

Feel free to comment. What do you think an extra card slot is worth?

I don't think this has anything much to do with that other thread
because blood is more useful on vampires than it is sitting in your
blood pool. (or else you wouldn't influence them)

Thanks,

Rob Grau

> make the card slot from Elder Library worth 1/10 of a pool per turn.

Assuming you get to play it on your first turn.
Statistically, it would be worth a bit less (75% - 66%, I'd guess) in
practice. (50% if it were played during any of the 10 turns with
equal probability - but that isn't the case).

It's cost is also increased by: 1 Master Phase Action (and is
increased *very* slightly by both uniqueness and being a location).

> Now, Dreams of the Sphinx:
>
> 2 Extra Card Slots, 1 Pool, Not more than three turns total.
>
> The difference here is that You only get the hand size bonus during the
> current turn, meaning that I've got to depreciate the pool value of "per
> turn" which I just used to mean "from turn to turn". Simple math comes
> to 1/6 of a pool, which I'll half to 1/12 of a pool per turn.
>
> The exact number is debatable, but I think anything between 1/6 - 1/12
> is a fair number to quote.

The effect is greater than the card slots. Dreams can also be used to
recoup the pool cost (on the same turn, even) via transfers, or (on a
subsequent turn) via the Edge. And, when used for the transfer, it also
allows you to control a vampire more quickly. Flexibility itself
increases the "power" of this card.

And, as above, the cost is more than just the pool: it costs a Master
Phase Action (and is unique).

> From this we can calculate the amount of pool it costs to play
> Aggressive Tactics - 2 Pool, 1 Card Slot, (D) Burnable. I've never
> played with the card so I don't know how long the card sticks around,
> but I'd guess it's high on the "Things to burn" list.
>
> The cost of -just- playing the card would be pool cost minus benefit.

Again: plus the Master Phase Action.

> Which if burned after one turn is 2 - (~1/10) or 1 and 9/10 pool.
> If burned after three turns is 2/3 - (~1/10) or ~4/7 pool per turn.
> At 20 turns the card is free given the benefit you have received, but
> the game isn't likely to last that long.
>
> Feel free to comment. What do you think an extra card slot is worth?
>
> I don't think this has anything much to do with that other thread
> because blood is more useful on vampires than it is sitting in your
> blood pool. (or else you wouldn't influence them)

I think that that's overstating things a good deal. Having a vampire
out (and full, temorarily) rather than uncontrolled is worth a
corresponding reduction in your pool. Once he's controlled, however,
he has many more options (and easier options) for gaining blood (not from
your pool) than you have for gaining pool (not from a vampire). Not
to mention the fact that he is still pretty valuable even when his blood
is reduced.

Hence the popularity of Blood Doll - used mainly to increase your
pool at the expense of your vampire's blood and only infrequently
the other way around.

Messages.Author: Rob Grau

Yes, the best ways to add/remove cards from player's hands are all master
phase actions, and that's probably what is going to make it impossible to
really quantify the "cost in pool" of the card slot in the hand. In the game
we don't fret over the exact opportunity cost of a master action, but you're
right it clearly figures into my pool cost per turn item. Anybody have some
sense of appropriate opportuntity cost for a master phase action? (ie how much
is the next best action worth in terms of pool?)

I was impressed at how just using Dreams for the card slots had a comparable

Yes it is an overstatement. I was hasty. Having now given it a little more
thought, it has to lie on some principle involving diminishing returns. If you
have 30 pool and no vampires, that pool is more valuable on a vampire,
decreasingly so with each transfer you make. And with 1 or 2 pool and
controlled vampires with blood dolls, it makes no sense to be transferring
pool to vamps. (along with the benefit that you pointed out over value of
vampires with a decreased number of blood counters).

Messages.Author: Derek S. Ray
Messages.Body:
Well, the basic master card is Ascendance, which means one master
phase action should, after all effects are considered, gain you one
pool. Obviously, not all master cards are created equal, but I'll bet
most of them can work out to roughly that. (Hunting Grounds cost two
to play, but will gain you over a long period of time - after you've
Blood Dolled three of those free vampire blood off, you've gained one
pool. I suspect that's a reasonably accurate assessment, too.)

>(Hunting Grounds cost two
>to play, but will gain you over a long period of time - after you've
>Blood Dolled three of those free vampire blood off, you've gained one
>pool.

Of course, that's now *two* master phase actions (the playing of the
Hunting Ground and the playing of the Blood Doll) in order to achieve a
gain of one pool, over a period of three turns, not forgetting that it
makes a vampire slightly more vulnerable by preventing them from being
at capacity - though only a little, of course.

If you only wanted pool, over those three turns, you could play
Ascendance three times and make a three pool profit, if card slots are
not an issue (as they would be in, say, a weenie Brujah rush deck).

However, the cost of the card slot is, of course, not the only thing to
consider. Blood Doll, whilst increasing the "cost" of the Hunting
Ground to make a profit, in terms of slots, MPAs etc., provides
flexibility in allowing you to put blood *back* on the vampire - useful
if you need just an extra blood to force an action through - say, it
allows you to afford an Earth Control or a Day Operation, something like
that. Using three Ascendances does not give you that option.
